Meta-analysis in R

A worked example: BCG vaccine and tuberculosis (13 RCTs)

Dr Gurpreet

2026-11-18

The question and the data

The data: 13 trials of BCG vaccine

Study Latitude (°) Allocation Vaccinated: TB / N Control: TB / N
Aronson, 1948 44 Random 4 / 123 11 / 139
Ferguson & Simes, 1949 55 Random 6 / 306 29 / 303
Rosenthal et al, 1960 42 Random 3 / 231 11 / 220
Hart & Sutherland, 1977 52 Random 62 / 13,598 248 / 12,867

Stein & Aronson, 1953 44 Alternate 180 / 1,541 372 / 1,451
Vandiviere et al, 1973 19 Random 8 / 2,545 10 / 629
TPT Madras, 1980 13 Random 505 / 88,391 499 / 88,391
Coetzee & Berjak, 1968 27 Random 29 / 7,499 45 / 7,277

PICO: Population = people in 13 trial settings · Intervention = BCG · Comparator = no vaccine · Outcome = TB cases. Trial sizes range from 262 to 176,782 participants, and sites span 13° to 55° latitude.

Step 1: Effect size for each trial

Study RR 95% CI
Aronson, 1948 0.41 0.13 to 1.26
Ferguson & Simes, 1949 0.20 0.09 to 0.49
Rosenthal et al, 1960 0.26 0.07 to 0.92
Hart & Sutherland, 1977 0.24 0.18 to 0.31
Frimodt-Moller et al, 1973 0.80 0.52 to 1.25
Stein & Aronson, 1953 0.46 0.39 to 0.54
Vandiviere et al, 1973 0.20 0.08 to 0.50
TPT Madras, 1980 1.01 0.89 to 1.14
Coetzee & Berjak, 1968 0.63 0.39 to 1.00
Rosenthal et al, 1961 0.25 0.15 to 0.43
Comstock et al, 1974 0.71 0.57 to 0.89
Comstock & Webster, 1969 1.56 0.37 to 6.53
Comstock et al, 1976 0.98 0.58 to 1.66

How to read

Risk ratio (RR) = risk of TB in vaccinated ÷ risk in controls. RR < 1 means the vaccine protects. We analyse log RR and back-transform for display.

What we infer

RRs range from 0.20 to 1.56. Most trials favour BCG, but by very different amounts: the first hint of heterogeneity.

Pooling the trials

Step 2: Common-effect vs random-effects

Model Pooled RR (95% CI) 95% prediction interval
Common effect 0.65 (0.60 to 0.70) —
Random effects 0.49 (0.34 to 0.70) 0.15 to 1.55

How to read

Common effect assumes all trials estimate one true RR. Random effects assumes true RRs vary between settings and estimates their average. The prediction interval is where a new trial’s true RR is likely to fall.

What we infer

BCG reduces TB risk by about 51% on average (RR 0.49). The common-effect CI is falsely narrow because it ignores between-trial variation. The prediction interval (0.15 to 1.55) crosses 1.

Step 3: Forest plot

Square = trial’s RR, size = weight. Line = its 95% CI.

Vertical line at 1 = no effect. Left favours BCG.

Diamond = pooled RR and CI. Dotted line = prediction interval.

x-axis is log scale: 0.5 and 2 are equally far from 1.

Forest plot: what we infer

Direction: 11 of 13 trials favour BCG.

Precision: several trials are non-significant alone, yet the pooled RR 0.49 (0.34 to 0.70) is clearly below 1.

Heterogeneity by eye: CIs often do not overlap (Hart & Sutherland 0.24 vs TPT Madras 1.01).

Weights are even (4–10%). Under common effect, TPT Madras alone would take 41%.

Heterogeneity

Step 4: How much do the trials disagree?

Statistic Estimate 95% CI
Cochran’s Q (df = 12) 152.23 p < 0.0001
τ² 0.31 0.12 to 1.11
τ 0.56 0.35 to 1.05
I² (%) 92.22 81.92 to 97.68
H² 12.86 5.53 to 43.07

How to read

Q tests “all trials share one effect”. I² = share of variability due to real differences (a proportion). τ² = between-trial variance on the log RR scale (an absolute amount).

What we infer

I² = 92%: almost all the spread is real, not chance. Even the lower CI bound (82%) is high. Pooling is still fine, but we must explain the heterogeneity.

Step 5: Meta-regression on latitude

How to read

Bubble = trial (size = weight). Line and band = fitted relation and its 95% CI. Dashed line = no effect. A slope means the moderator explains heterogeneity.

What we infer

Each degree from the equator multiplies RR by 0.97. Little effect near the equator; strong protection above 50°. Latitude explains 76% of τ²; I² falls from 92% to 68%.

Across-study (ecological) association. Latitude is a proxy, e.g. for exposure to environmental mycobacteria.

Small-study effects

Step 6: Funnel plots

How to read: effect (x) vs standard error (y, inverted: big trials at top). Expect a symmetric funnel; a gap in a bottom corner suggests missing small trials. Grey zones = statistically significant results.

What we infer: large trials are spread widely (heterogeneity, not bias). Small trials sit in both shaded and white zones, so only a mild hint of asymmetry and no clear sign of missing null trials.

Step 7: Egger’s test and trim-and-fill

Test Result
Egger’s regression t = -1.40, p = 0.19
Begg’s rank correlation Kendall’s τ = 0.03, p = 0.95
Trim-and-fill: studies imputed 1 (right side)
Trim-and-fill: adjusted RR 0.52 (0.37 to 0.74)

How to read: Egger tests whether small trials give systematically different results. Trim-and-fill imputes “missing” trials (open circles) and re-pools.

Use these tests only with ≥ 10 studies. Asymmetry ≠ publication bias: heterogeneity alone can distort a funnel.

What we infer: no strong evidence of small-study effects. Adjusting moves RR only from 0.49 to 0.52.

Sensitivity analysis

Step 8: Leave-one-out

How to read

Each row = re-analysis without that trial. Dashed line and band = original RR and CI. Red line = no effect. Labels = I² after removal.

What we infer

RR stays between 0.45 and 0.53; no CI crosses 1. Robust. Dropping TPT Madras gives 0.45 (I² 87%); dropping Hart & Sutherland gives 0.53.

I² stays above 85% whatever is removed: heterogeneity is not one outlier.

Step 9: Influence diagnostics

How to read

One dot per trial. rstudent beyond ±2 = outlier. cook.d / dffits = shift in pooled result if removed. QE.del = Q after removal. Red = flagged as influential.

What we infer

0 trials flagged. Hart & Sutherland (Cook’s d 0.23) and TPT Madras (0.20) matter most; removing them cuts Q from 152 to 97 and 68.

Step 10: Baujat plot

How to read

x = contribution to heterogeneity. y = influence on the pooled result. Top-right trials do both and deserve a closer look.

What we infer

Trials 4 (Hart & Sutherland, 52°) and 8 (TPT Madras, 13°) sit top-right, at opposite latitudes: the same story as the meta-regression.

Summary

Results at a glance

Item Result
Trials (k) 13
Pooled RR, random effects (95% CI) 0.49 (0.34 to 0.70)
95% prediction interval 0.15 to 1.55
I² 92%
τ² 0.31
Latitude: R² of meta-regression 76%
Egger’s test p 0.19
Leave-one-out RR range 0.45 to 0.53

Take-home messages

1. BCG reduces TB risk by about half on average (RR 0.49).

2. Heterogeneity is very high (I² 92%). Always report the prediction interval, not only the CI.

3. Look for why trials differ: latitude explains about three-quarters of it.

4. Funnel asymmetry ≠ publication bias. Here there is no strong evidence of small-study effects.

5. Sensitivity analyses show the conclusion does not rest on any single trial.
